records.name: Bremen
records.current_summary:
Bremen has no trans-specific statute, ordinance or enforcement series of its own on file. The city-state operates Germany's federal framework: the Self-Determination Act, in force since 1 November 2024, remains operative as of September 2026, and registry changes run through Bremen's own offices; federal criminal law and the general equality act apply unchanged.

Two framework-level developments matter for trans people everywhere in Germany through state competence over prisons: a July 2026 court-ordered placement of a trans-woman-registered prisoner in a men's prison (the widely reported 'Liebich' case) drove three eastern states into a Bundesrat initiative to tighten the Self-Determination Act; and a March 2026 constitutional-law survey found most Länder anchoring newly reformed prison-placement codes to the registry sex entry — Bremen is not among the states named as having rewritten its code, and no Bremen-specific detention finding is on file.

Framework analysis (Verfassungsblog, 18 Mar 2026) of German state prison-placement rules under the Self-Determination Act: all Länder tie placement to the prisoner's legal gender; § 6(1) SBGG lets state law override the entry, and many Länder have enacted exception clauses — some abstract (all inmates), some criticised as trans-targeted. Bremen has no placement statute of its own, so this national framework is the operative standard for inmate-placement questions.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Germany - Wikipedia
sources.claim: Germany's federal Self-Determination Act, the framework a trans visitor to Bremen stands under, passed parliament by 374-251 and took effect on 1 November 2024: adults over 18 can change their legal gender by self-determination, and the change is entered in the civil registry, i.e. handled through offices including Bremen's own. The article records that years of self-identification apply to adults without requiring the previous medical/court pathway, and that same-sex marriage has been legal since 1 October 2017. It confirms no Bremen-specific deviation: the city-state operates the unchanged federal act as of the article's coverage.

sources.title: Homosexualität in Deutschland - de.wikipedia.org
sources.claim: German Wikipedia's overview of homosexuality in Germany (the federal legal framework Bremen operates under) records that Germany's first Christopher Street Days were held in 1979 in Berlin, with 400 partly masked participants, and in Bremen - making Bremen one of the two original host cities of public LGBT street demonstrations in the country. The article also documents the federal criminal-law history in which Bremen's current status sits, including the Nazi-era tightening of Section 175a with penitentiary terms of up to ten years and the persecution of men including forced castration in prisons. No Bremen-specific statute or enforcement is claimed anywhere in the article, consistent with the record's finding that Bremen relies on the federal framework.

records.name: Hamburg
records.current_summary:
Hamburg has no hostile-offence series, ordinance or event-security finding on file; risk tracks Germany's federal framework, with one local exception that is institutional rather than social: Hamburg is among the Länder whose newly reformed prison-placement rules have entered into force, tying inmate placement to the civil-registry sex entry — a March 2026 constitutional-law survey counts it alongside the first wave of rewrites (a Rhineland-Palatinate code effective 1 March 2026, Bavaria, Saxony) and argues the registry-anchored approach is constitutionally avoidable and in part doubtful on fundamental-rights grounds.

The framework around it moved in July 2026: a court-ordered placement of a trans-woman-registered prisoner in a men's facility (the reported 'Liebich' case, arising in the northeast, corroborated by multiple wire reports of 15-17 July 2026) sharpened pressure that produced a Bundesrat initiative to tighten the federal Self-Determination Act, itself in force since November 2024. For a visitor, detention-time placement — not street-level hostility — is where Hamburg's documented divergence lies, and it is a resident-facing machinery a arrested visitor would enter.
records.current_localsOnly: Hamburg's reformed prison-placement rule (in force alongside the 2025-26 wave of Länder reforms) and registry-office administration of the federal self-determination law concern residents and detainees, not visitors.

Framework analysis (Verfassungsblog, 18 Mar 2026) of trans prisoner placement under the Self-Determination Act (SBGG, in force 1 Nov 2024): legal gender entry governs unless state law provides otherwise; constitutional doubts voiced about trans-targeted exception clauses. Anchors the July 2026 Neubrandenburg case (court-ordered male-prison placement despite legal gender change, DW/Telegraph 15-17 Jul 2026) that drove Länder action; Hamburg-specific enforcement findings remain none on file.

sources.title: Transgender rights in Germany - Wikipedia
sources.claim: Since the federal Self-Determination Act came into effect on 1 November 2024, adults in Germany - including in Hamburg, whose registry offices process the change - can change their legal gender and first name in the civil registry without a psychological evaluation or court order, replacing the earlier court/evaluation pathway with gender self-identification. The Act standardized trans, inter and non-binary regulation in a single law and revised the Third Gender Act provisions; birth-register parent entries still record the old gender (e.g. a trans woman listed as 'father'), though a 'parent' option is now available on birth certificates. This registry-gender anchor is the same administrative basis the record's prison-placement divergence turns on.

sources.title: Homosexualität in Deutschland - de.wikipedia.org
sources.claim: German Wikipedia's federal overview carries a Hamburg subsection: Hamburg is described as northern Germany's centre of the gay scene, with its gay quarter in the district of St. Georg, where a number of gay and lesbian bars, cafés and clubs operate off the Reeperbahn 'Kiez', and it records the 2003 episode in which Hamburg's then First Mayor Ole von Beust, after an alleged blackmail attempt involving deputy mayor Ronald Schill, did not deny his homosexuality. For this record the article documents a socially embedded and institutionally visible LGBT presence in Hamburg - the local context against which the registry-anchored prison-placement rule, the record's only documented divergence, operates.

sources.title: Studie zu Lebenslagen und Erfahrungen von LSBTIQ* „Queer durch NRW“ (Ministerium für Kinder, Jugend, Familie, Gleichstellung, Flucht und Integration NRW / chancen.nrw)
sources.claim: The North Rhine-Westphalian state ministry page records that on 25 April 2025 the Land government published the study „Queer durch NRW – Lebenslagen und Erfahrungen von LSBTIQ*“, the first comprehensive dataset on the living situations of lesbian, gay, bisexual, trans*, inter*, queer and non-binary people (LSBTIQ*) in the Land. The study combined quantitative online surveys — more than 5,000 LSBTIQ* respondents, 775 relatives and over 5,000 professionals — with qualitative focus groups and expert interviews, covering three areas: discrimination, violence and safety; health, care and ageing; and integration, migration and flight. It was commissioned under Landtag resolution Drucksache 18/6360 to develop the state's „Aktionsplan für Vielfalt und gegen Homo- und Transfeindlichkeit“ on a broader data basis. This gives the record its first genuinely Nordrhein-Westfalen-specific source with Land-level findings on discrimination, violence and safety affecting trans* people — relevant to visitor exposure because the Land enacted no trans statute and the state's anti-homo/transphobia action plan now rests on this data.

records.name: Rheinland-Pfalz
records.current_summary:
Rhineland-Palatinate replaced its prison-execution code with a new § 17, in force 1 March 2026, anchoring inmate placement to the civil-register sex entry — the first reform of the wave that, per a March 2026 constitutional-law survey, made such registry-based placement the majority practice among the Länder. The same essay, written against the July 2026 case in which a prisoner whose legal gender had been changed under the federal Self-Determination Act was sent to a men's prison, argues the registry standard is constitutionally avoidable and some Land versions doubtful, defending inclusive pre-correction placement as constitutional.

These are detained-person rules in a field that is a Land competence; no other Rhineland-Palatine trans statute, ordinance, enforcement series or event-security finding survives in the records, so visitor exposure tracks the national framework.

Verfassungsblog analysis (18 Mar 2026) of the new § 17 Landesjustizvollzugsgesetz Rheinland-Pfalz, in force 1 March 2026, which anchors inmate placement to the legally recorded gender entry with a general, abstract exception clause open to all prisoners (not targeted at trans people as such). RLP is the Land that took the (now absolute) majority of states past the point of modernising placement rules unchanged since the 1970s. The piece raises constitutional doubts about the alternative, trans-targeted exception clauses used by other states; direct relevance for RLP visitors facing detention placement decisions.

Cites Saarland's single-cell-with-en-suite-shower accommodation as a positive practice model for trans inmates; framework-relevant to Saarland, which has no separate placement statute.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Germany (Wikipedia)
sources.claim: The page records that Saarland's state constitution was amended in 2011 so that its anti-discrimination provisions explicitly include sexual orientation and gender identity, one of only five Lander constitutions to carry such a clause (Berlin since 1995, Brandenburg since 1992, Bremen since 2001, Saarland since 2011, Thuringia since 1993; Saxony-Anhalt in the public sector since 1997). It further records that Saarland, with Hesse, Berlin, Bremen and Schleswig-Holstein, tabled a joint Bundesrat motion for a ban on conversion therapy, presented in plenary on 12 April 2019, with Saxony, Saxony-Anhalt and Thuringia agreeing and Bavaria offering modified support. Gives the state-constitutional protection against discrimination on grounds of gender identity that a trans visitor stands under within Saarland.

sources.title: Transgender rights in Germany (Wikipedia)
sources.claim: The page states that hate speech on the basis of sexual orientation and gender identity is not banned nationwide in Germany, but that some states have laws banning all forms of discrimination in their constitutions - Berlin, Brandenburg, Bremen, Saarland and Thuringia - and that in those states hate speech based on both sexual orientation and gender identity is prohibited. For Saarland this is a jurisdiction-specific enforcement difference: transphobic hate speech is prohibited under the state constitution, unlike in most of Germany, and the federal General Act on Equal Treatment (in force since 18 August 2006) bans discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity in employment, education, health services and the provision of goods and services.

sources.title: Jens Spahn will Pseudotherapien gegen Homosexualität verbieten
sources.claim: Zeit Online (10 April 2019) reports that parallel to Federal Health Minister Jens Spahn's announced plan to ban so-called conversion therapies, Hesse, Berlin, Bremen, Saarland and Schleswig-Holstein planned to present a joint Bundesrat motion (Entschließungsantrag) for a ban that same week. Nails Saarland by name as one of the five tabling states in the run-up to the 12 April 2019 Bundesrat plenary presentation recorded by Wikipedia's LGBTQ rights in Germany page; the federal ban was subsequently approved by the Bundestag on 7 May 2020.
